Tyranny of the majority can hurt the majority itself in the long run.

Power shared among legislature, executive and judiciary is called ____ distribution.
When two or more parties form an alliance to govern together, the result is a ____ government.
Describe the ethnic composition of Sri Lanka.
questions.answer: Sri Lanka has two major social groups: SINHALA-speakers (74%) and TAMIL-speakers (18%). Tamils are further split into Sri Lankan Tamils (13%, native to the island) and Indian Tamils (5%, brought as plantation workers in the colonial period). Most Sinhala-speakers are BUDDHIST; most Tamils are HINDU or MUSLIM. About 7% of Sri Lankans are CHRISTIANS, drawn from both Sinhala and Tamil communities.

questions.question: List the major MAJORITARIAN measures taken by Sri Lankan governments.
questions.answer: (i) 1956 — Act recognising SINHALA as the only official language, disregarding Tamil. (ii) Preferential policies favouring Sinhala applicants for university positions and government jobs. (iii) A new constitution stipulating that the state shall protect and foster BUDDHISM. These measures together created Tamil alienation and ultimately civil war.

questions.question: List four key features of the Belgian power-sharing model.
questions.answer: (i) The number of Dutch and French-speaking ministers in the central government must be EQUAL. (ii) Many central powers are devolved to STATE GOVERNMENTS of the two regions, which are NOT subordinate to the centre. (iii) BRUSSELS has a separate government with EQUAL representation of both communities. (iv) A 'COMMUNITY GOVERNMENT' is elected by people of one language community (Dutch / French / German) regardless of where they live, and looks after cultural / educational / language matters.

questions.question: What is the difference between PRUDENTIAL and MORAL reasons for power-sharing?
questions.answer: PRUDENTIAL reasons stress that power-sharing brings BETTER OUTCOMES — it reduces conflict between social groups, prevents violence and ensures political stability. It is based on careful calculation of gains and losses. MORAL reasons say that power-sharing is the VERY SPIRIT OF DEMOCRACY itself — people have a right to be consulted on how they are to be governed. While prudential reasons look at consequences, moral reasons emphasise the very act of power-sharing as valuable.

questions.question: Explain the four major forms of power-sharing in modern democracies.
questions.answer: (i) HORIZONTAL — among legislature, executive and judiciary at the same level (checks and balances). (ii) VERTICAL — between central / state / local governments. (iii) Among different SOCIAL GROUPS — e.g. Belgium's Community Government; reserved constituencies for SC / ST in India. (iv) Among POLITICAL PARTIES, pressure groups and movements — e.g. coalition governments; trade and industry associations influencing policy.

questions.question: Compare the Belgian and Sri Lankan approaches to managing ethnic diversity. What lessons do they teach about power-sharing?
questions.answer: Both Belgium and Sri Lanka are small countries with sharp ethnic and linguistic divisions. They started with similar problems but chose OPPOSITE paths. SRI LANKA adopted MAJORITARIAN measures: a 1956 Sinhala-only law, preferential job and university policies for the Sinhala majority, and a constitution that fostered Buddhism. The Tamil minority was alienated; their demand for autonomy was repeatedly denied; by the 1980s they demanded a separate Tamil Eelam. The country slid into a civil war that lasted until 2009 — costing thousands of lives, displacement, and a setback to the social, cultural and economic life of the nation. BELGIUM took the opposite path. It RECOGNISED its diversity and amended the constitution four times between 1970 and 1993 to share power: equal Dutch–French ministers in the central government; powerful state governments not subordinate to the centre; a separate Brussels government with equal representation of both communities; and a unique COMMUNITY GOVERNMENT for cultural / language matters elected by each language community. The arrangements are complicated, but they have AVOIDED civic strife and even kept the country together — Brussels was made the capital of the European Union. LESSONS: (i) majoritarianism may look attractive in the short run, but it undermines national unity and hurts the majority too; (ii) carefully designed power-sharing — even if complicated — produces stable, prosperous democracies; (iii) constitutional and institutional arrangements matter more than slogans of unity.
questions.explanation: Belgium vs Sri Lanka: contrasting models.

questions.question: 'Power-sharing is the very spirit of democracy.' Discuss this statement, giving examples of horizontal, vertical, social and party power-sharing.
questions.answer: Democracy means rule by the people — and the people are not one undivided block but a collection of social groups, regions and interests. So power-sharing is not just one feature of democracy among many; it IS democracy. Without it, an elected government can quickly become tyrannical. There are at least four forms: (i) HORIZONTAL — among legislature, executive and judiciary (checks and balances). For example, in India the Supreme Court can strike down laws of Parliament; the executive is answerable to the Lok Sabha. (ii) VERTICAL — between Union, State and Local governments, with the Constitution clearly assigning different powers to each. (iii) Among SOCIAL GROUPS — the Belgian Community Government; reserved seats for SCs and STs in Indian assemblies; arrangements for women's representation. (iv) Among POLITICAL PARTIES, pressure groups and movements — coalition governments; trade unions, business associations and farmer movements influencing policy. PRUDENTIAL reasons (avoiding conflict, ensuring stability) AND MORAL reasons (people have a right to be consulted) both support power-sharing. Sri Lanka's experience shows what happens when power is hoarded by the majority; Belgium's experience shows what is possible when it is shared. The chapter therefore concludes that, in any genuine democracy, political power must be distributed among as many citizens as possible.
